body:
Religious teaching became accessible to wider audiences

One important cultural contribution of Jainism and Buddhism was the communication of religious ideas in languages understood by ordinary listeners. This widened the audience for teaching beyond people trained in the language of Vedic ritual.

The Vedas were preserved in Vedic Sanskrit. Jain and Buddhist teachers, by contrast, communicated through discussion and instruction in spoken regional languages. Prakrit is a broad term for related Middle Indo-Aryan languages and language forms. Magadhi was associated with the Magadha region.

Pali became especially important as a literary language of early Buddhist scriptures. Jain literature was preserved in Prakrit varieties and, in later periods, also in Sanskrit and regional languages. The use of accessible language helped teachings circulate among merchants, householders, workers and other lay audiences.

The Buddha's spoken teaching should not be identified exclusively with the later literary language of every Buddhist manuscript. Early Buddhist traditions were transmitted orally and preserved in more than one linguistic setting.

Buddhist literature and the Tripitaka

The Buddha taught orally, through sermons, conversations and discussions. His followers preserved and organised these teachings, initially through memorisation and recitation. Over time, Buddhist textual collections were written down.

A major collection is the Tripitaka, also called Tipitaka, meaning 3 baskets or collections:

CollectionPrincipal content
Vinaya PitakaRules and discipline for monks and nuns
Sutta PitakaDiscourses, teachings and related compositions
Abhidhamma PitakaSystematic philosophical and doctrinal analysis

The Jataka stories describe former lives of the Buddha according to Buddhist tradition. They often communicate lessons through accounts of generosity, compassion, honesty and other qualities. Their stories influenced literature and visual art, including carvings on stupa gateways.

The Therigatha, a collection of verses attributed to early Buddhist nuns, is especially important for its expression of women's experiences and religious aspirations. It forms part of the Buddhist textual tradition preserved within the Sutta Pitaka.

Jain literature and the preservation of teaching

Jain teachings were also transmitted orally for centuries before being organised in surviving written collections. The Agamas are important Jain scriptures, particularly in the Shvetambara textual tradition. Jain writers also contributed to literary traditions in Prakrit, Sanskrit and regional languages.

Stories and dialogues made abstract teachings easier to understand. A narrative about non-attachment, for example, could communicate Jain principles through familiar problems involving possessions, desires and moral choices.

Monasteries as centres of learning

Religious communities needed to preserve teachings, train new members, discuss ethical questions and pass knowledge between generations. Monasteries consequently served as places of instruction, recitation and debate, as well as residence.

Buddhist monks and nuns became teachers, while lay followers could attend discussions and receive instruction. Jain monastic communities likewise preserved religious teachings and developed traditions of scholarship. In later centuries, libraries associated with Jain religious institutions helped preserve manuscripts.

An important later development was Nalanda Mahavihara in present-day Bihar. It developed into a major Buddhist monastic and scholarly institution from about the 5th century CE and continued for several centuries. Its significance lies in organised learning, residential instruction and the circulation of knowledge among scholars from different regions.

The rise of Jainism and Buddhism belongs mainly to the 6th century BCE setting, whereas the major institutional development of Nalanda Mahavihara belongs to a much later period, beginning around the 5th century CE.

From speech to enduring traditions

Oral teaching enabled teachers to reach immediate audiences. Recitation helped communities remember teachings. Written manuscripts allowed longer collections to be preserved, copied, studied and carried to other regions. Monasteries and networks of teachers supported this continued transmission.

Prelims focus

  • Prakrit refers to Middle Indo-Aryan language forms; Magadhi was associated with Magadha.
  • Pali is an important language of early Buddhist literature.
  • Vinaya concerns discipline, Sutta concerns discourses, and Abhidhamma concerns philosophical analysis.
  • Jataka stories concern former lives of the Buddha in Buddhist tradition.
  • Nalanda Mahavihara, in Bihar, became a major learning centre from about the 5th century CE.
  • Trap: Pali is a language; it is not the name of a writing script.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 7, 'New Questions and Ideas', printed pp. 65–72, and Chapter 9, 'Vital Villages, Thriving Towns', pp. 89–90; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, 'How Buddhist texts were prepared and preserved', 'The spread of Jainism' and 'The Therigatha', printed pp. 86–94; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Archaeological Site of Nalanda Mahavihara at Nalanda, Bihar', Outstanding Universal Value, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Vernacular Communication, Religious Literature and Education

body:
New religious activity encouraged monumental art

The expansion of Buddhist and Jain communities encouraged the construction of places for worship, residence, teaching and remembrance. Religious donations supported builders, stoneworkers, sculptors and other craftspeople. Architecture and images became important ways of communicating beliefs to people who might not read religious manuscripts.

The development was gradual. Different regions, patrons and periods produced different forms of monuments. Religious art also incorporated local artistic traditions rather than emerging in a completely separate cultural world.

The Buddhist stupa

A stupa is a mound-like monument associated in Buddhism with relics, remembrance and worship. Relics might include bodily remains or objects connected with a revered teacher. Stupas also served votive and commemorative purposes.

The practice of erecting funerary mounds was older than Buddhism. Buddhists gave the stupa particular religious significance, but the basic idea of a mound over remains was not exclusively a Buddhist invention.

Important architectural terms include:

  • Anda: the rounded or hemispherical mound of the stupa.
  • Harmika: a small railing-like structure above the dome.
  • Yashti: the central mast rising above the harmika.
  • Chhatra or chhatri: an umbrella-like element associated with the mast.
  • Vedika: a railing marking the sacred area.
  • Torana: an entrance gateway, often decorated with carvings.
  • Pradakshinapatha: a path used for clockwise circumambulation, with the sacred monument kept on the right.

Important stupa centres

Sanchi in present-day Madhya Pradesh is among the most important surviving centres of Buddhist art and architecture. Its earliest major stupa was associated with Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE. The original brick structure was enlarged and embellished in later centuries. Its carved gateways depict religious stories and scenes of social life.

Bharhut, also in Madhya Pradesh, is known for early Buddhist relief sculpture, while Amaravati in present-day Andhra Pradesh became an important centre of elaborately carved stupa art.

Early symbols and later images

In many early Buddhist sculptures, the Buddha was represented through symbols rather than a human figure. The symbol often pointed to a specific event or religious idea:

  • Bodhi tree: enlightenment.
  • Empty seat or throne: the Buddha's presence or meditation.
  • Wheel of Dhamma: the first sermon at Sarnath.
  • Stupa: remembrance of the Buddha and, in some representations, his final passing away.
  • Footprints: the presence or spiritual journey of the Buddha.

These symbols should not be confused with the later development of human images of the Buddha. From around the 1st century CE, Mathura and Gandhara became important centres of Buddha-image production. Mathura drew strongly on indigenous sculptural traditions, while Gandhara also displayed Hellenistic artistic influences.

Chaityas, viharas and rock-cut architecture

Chaitya halls were spaces associated with religious worship and congregation, commonly with a stupa at one end in early Buddhist cave architecture. A vihara, by contrast, primarily provided residential accommodation for monks and, in many cases, space for instruction.

Rock-cut Buddhist establishments developed in western India, including sites at Bhaja, Karle and Ajanta in present-day Maharashtra. Ajanta is particularly celebrated for its paintings and sculptures depicting Buddhist themes. Its artistic activity belongs to more than one period, including an early phase around the 2nd–1st centuries BCE and a major later phase around the 5th century CE.

Jain communities also sponsored sculptures and religious establishments. Images of Tirthankaras are important in Jain art, with early examples found at places such as Mathura. Thus, artistic development was not confined to a single religious tradition.

Prelims focus

  • Sanchi and Bharhut are in Madhya Pradesh; Amaravati is in Andhra Pradesh.
  • The earliest major stupa at Sanchi is associated with Ashoka.
  • Torana means gateway; vedika means railing; anda means dome.
  • The Wheel of Dhamma symbolises the Buddha's first sermon at Sarnath.
  • Chaitya commonly denotes a worship space; vihara denotes a monastic residence.
  • Trap: The tradition of building funerary mounds did not begin exclusively with Buddhism.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, 'Stupas' and 'Sculpture', printed pp. 95–102; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 3, 'Arts of the Mauryan Period', printed pp. 19–26, and Chapter 4, 'Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture', printed pp. 27–38; Archaeological Survey of India, 'Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi', consulted 18 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi' and 'Ajanta Caves', Outstanding Universal Value, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Stupas, Monasteries and Religious Art

body:
Gujarat in the history of early religious movements

Gujarat has several important connections with the spread and preservation of Jain and Buddhist traditions. These include Jain literary activity, Buddhist monuments, Ashokan inscriptions and commercial centres linked to wider networks of movement and exchange.

Valabhi and the preservation of Jain scriptures

Valabhi, in present-day Gujarat, is particularly important for the history of Jain literature. Jain teachings had been transmitted orally for centuries. Around the 5th century CE, an important compilation of Jain scriptures was undertaken at Valabhi, especially within the Shvetambara tradition.

This was a major event in the preservation and organisation of the Jain textual tradition. It should not be understood as the moment when Jainism began or as evidence that Mahavira personally wrote the surviving scriptures.

Devni Mori: a Buddhist site in Gujarat

Devni Mori, near Shamlaji in present-day Aravalli district, is an important early historic Buddhist site. Its remains include a stupa and a monastery associated with the 3rd–4th centuries CE.

An inscribed relic casket found at the site is associated with relics identified in the inscription as those of the Buddha. Devni Mori therefore provides a concrete Gujarat example of Buddhist monastic establishment and relic-related stupa worship.

Girnar and Ashoka's moral message

Near Junagadh, at the foot of Girnar, are major rock edicts of Ashoka dating to approximately the 3rd century BCE. They form part of the ruler's wider effort to communicate his principles of dhamma.

Ashoka's dhamma encouraged ethical conduct, respect for elders, humane treatment of others and regard for different religious traditions. His inscriptions generally communicated these principles to a broad population rather than laying down only the rules of Buddhist monastic life.

The major Ashokan rock edicts in this region are associated with the Prakrit language and Brahmi script. Language and script are distinct: a language supplies words and grammar, whereas a script supplies written characters.

Ashoka's dhamma and the Buddha's Dhamma are historically connected, but should not be treated as identical sets of teachings. Ashoka's public edicts presented a practical moral message for his subjects.

Trade and religious connections

Bharuch in Gujarat was known to ancient Greek writers as Barygaza. Accounts of its maritime commerce describe the movement of goods such as cotton, silk, agate and carnelian, along with imports from other regions. This illustrates Gujarat's participation in extensive commercial networks during the early historic period.

Merchants and routes were important to the wider movement of people and ideas. However, it would be inaccurate to say that Jainism or Buddhism alone created the trade conducted through Bharuch. Religious and commercial developments interacted with an economy that had several independent foundations.

A chronological view of the changes

The continuing social and cultural influence

Jainism and Buddhism made lasting contributions in several related areas:

  • Ethical values: Jain ahimsa and Buddhist compassion strengthened traditions of self-restraint, non-injury and humane treatment.
  • Religious participation: Monastic communities offered a form of spiritual association that did not depend entirely on hereditary priestly status, although social inequalities continued outside and within wider religious life.
  • Language and literature: Prakrit and Pali traditions, together with later Sanskrit and regional-language writing, preserved extensive bodies of teaching and narrative literature.
  • Institutions: Monasteries provided settings for residence, instruction, debate and preservation of knowledge.
  • Art and architecture: Stupas, rock-cut chaityas, viharas, paintings and sculptures became important expressions of religious and artistic life.
  • Regional and international connections: Buddhism spread through routes connecting India with Sri Lanka, Central Asia, East Asia and Southeast Asia. Jainism continued to develop strong traditions in several Indian regions, including Gujarat.

These contributions accumulated over many centuries. They did not transform every community in the same way or cause existing religious and social practices to disappear. The most accurate understanding is one of interaction, adaptation and continuity among different traditions.

Prelims focus

  • Valabhi, Gujarat: important compilation of Jain scriptures around the 5th century CE.
  • Devni Mori, Aravalli: Buddhist stupa and monastery near Shamlaji.
  • Girnar, Junagadh: major rock edicts of Ashoka.
  • Bharuch: known as Barygaza in ancient Greek accounts of trade.
  • Prakrit is a language category; Brahmi is a script.
  • Trap: Do not confuse Valabhi's Jain textual association with Devni Mori's Buddhist monuments.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 7, 'New Questions and Ideas', printed pp. 69–72, and Chapter 9, 'Vital Villages, Thriving Towns', pp. 92–94; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, 'Kings, Farmers and Towns', printed pp. 32–34, and Theme 4, 'Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings', pp. 88–90; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 4, 'Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture', printed p. 32; Gujarat Tourism, 'Dev Ni Mori' and 'Ashok Edicts', consulted 18 November 2026; Government of Gujarat, Aravalli District, 'Devni Mori', and Junagadh District, 'Ashok Shilalekh', consulted 18 November 2026.]
